Commercial building at 15 Phillip Street in Raffles Place for sale at $91 mil
article:
A 10-storey commercial building at 15 Phillip Street in Raffles Place has been put up for sale through an expression of interest (EOI) at a guide price of $91 million.

Also known as Tan Ean Keam Building, it sits on 358.3 sq m (approximately 3,857 sq ft) site, with a coffee shop occupying the basement, first and second floors.

The eventual buyer can opt to either carry out asset enhancement works or redevelop it to “fully optimise” its unutilised gross floor area, said sole marketing agent ETC, a member of Realion Group, on Oct 23.

Under the URA Master Plan 2025, the site is zoned for commercial use with a plot ratio of 15 and a building height control of more than 50 storeys.

The property falls outside the areas subject to URA's restrictions on the strata subdivision of commercial space. This means the commercial redevelopment project may potentially be considered for strata sale in the future, according to ETC.

Swee Shou Fern, head of investment advisory at ETC, said there is potential for building signage and naming rights, which may appeal to companies looking to establish their corporate headquarters in Raffles Place. Owner-occupiers can also have greater control over their premises and occupancy costs.

In Singapore’s office investment market, smaller commercial assets in strategic locations continue to attract interest from investors seeking a more manageable price tag, Swee added.

"Such prized assets are tightly held and there is hardly any available for sale at under $100 million," she noted.

Located in the CBD, 15 Phillip Street is surrounded by commercial developments including CapitaSpring , Republic Plaza , UOB Plaza , One Raffles Place and OCBC Centre . Other nearby buildings include Royal One Phillip, Royal Group Building and Grand Building .

The property is within walking distance of Raffles Place MRT interchange, serving the North-South and East-West lines, as well as Telok Ayer MRT Station on the Downtown Line. It is also close to dining, retail and other amenities in the CBD.

As a commercial property, the acquisition is not subject to additional buyer's stamp duty, and there are no restrictions on foreign ownership.

The EOI exercise will close at 3pm on Nov 25.

title: AI firms boost office leasing demand as CBD Grade A rents climb 2% in 3Q2026
article:
Artificial intelligence (AI) companies are emerging as a growing source of office leasing demand in Singapore, adding to an already resilient market led by financial services, professional services and technology firms.

The demand comes as Core CBD Grade A office rents climbed 2% quarter-on-quarter (q-o-q) to $12.75 psf per month in 3Q2026, up from 0.8% in the preceding quarter, according to CBRE. This was the strongest quarterly rental increase since 3Q2022.

Meanwhile, the Urban Redevelopment Authority's (URA) broader office rental index for the Central Region rose 0.8% q-o-q in 3Q2026, matching the increase in 2Q2026.

Financial services remained the largest source of office leasing demand, accounting for 29% of new CBD leases in the first nine months of 2026, followed by professional services at 19% and technology at 16%, according to Cushman & Wakefield (C&W).

AI companies are also emerging as an increasingly significant source of demand, ranging from smaller firms taking up flexible workspaces to larger occupiers seeking dedicated premises in prime office buildings, says Tricia Song, CBRE head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia.

For instance, Anthropic has reportedly committed to 100 desks at The Executive Centre in Ocean Financial Centre , while Manus AI is understood to be taking up about 10,357 sq ft, or half of the flexible workspace operated by Industrious at Keppel South Central.

According to June Chua, Newmark's senior managing director and head of Singapore leasing, some technology and AI firms are moving from serviced offices into their own premises, signalling a deeper commitment to Singapore and the region.

Sierra AI has reportedly leased about 10,000 sq ft of dedicated office space at Keppel South Central, while OpenAI is in advanced negotiations for approximately 120,000 sq ft across five floors at Shaw Tower. This would represent a substantial expansion from OpenAI's current footprint of about 100 desks at The Work Project's CapitaSpring facility, says JLL.

Office Rental Indices

The Downtown Core remained the most active office submarket, recording about 0.1 million sq ft of net demand in 3Q2026, accounting for 53% of islandwide net demand during the quarter, says Wong Xian Yang, C&W head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia.

"This marks its sixth consecutive quarter of positive net demand, likely supported by higher take-up at new developments such as Shaw Tower and Keppel South Central, particularly from technology occupiers," adds Wong.

Meanwhile, islandwide office vacancy fell to 10% in 3Q2026 from 11% in the preceding quarter, its lowest level since 1Q2024.

The decline reflected both resilient occupier demand and the withdrawal of existing office space from the market for redevelopment, says CBRE's Song.

According to URA data, occupied office space rose by 17,000 sq m (close to 183,000 sq ft) in 3Q2026, while the overall office stock contracted by 72,000 sq m (775,000 sq ft).

CBRE attributes much of the contraction to the likely withdrawal of office space at 79 Anson and HarbourFront Centre for redevelopment.

The tightening was particularly evident in the premium CBD office segment, where vacancy fell to 2.6% from 3.3% in 2Q2026, notes CBRE's Song.

According to JLL, only two non-strata office developments are expected to enter the market over the next two years: the refurbished Robinson Point by end-2026 and Newport Tower in 2027.

URA data shows that about 94,000 sq m of gross office space is scheduled for completion in 2027, before supply rises to 319,000 sq m in 2028.

With limited new office supply expected before 2028, consultants anticipate further rental growth.

CBRE's Song expects Core CBD Grade A office rents to rise by more than 5% in 2026, the strongest annual growth since 2022.

C&W's Wong maintains his forecast of 4% to 5% growth in CBD Grade A office rents for the full year. Similarly, Newmark's Chua expects premium and Grade A office rents to rise by 4% to 5% this year.

title: Tuan Sing is buying Westgate Tower in Jurong Lake District for $600 mil
article:
Real estate development, investment and hospitality group Tuan Sing Holdings Limited will purchase premium Grade A office property Westgate Tower in Jurong Lake District at an agreed property value of $600 million — a discount of 6.25% to its latest valuation.

Its wholly-owned subsidiary Greenlane Land has inked a sale and purchase agreement to fully acquire two entities — Westgate Commercial Pte Ltd and Westgate Tower Pte Ltd — that collectively own all the commercial office units in the property located at 1 Gateway Drive.

Westgate Tower spans about 305,000 sq ft of net lettable area across 20 storeys, comprising 295 strata-titled office units with a committed occupancy rate of around 90%.

It is part of a mixed-use development that includes the seven-storey Westgate Mall, with a site area of 17,589.6 sq m (about 189,333 sq ft) and a 99-year leasehold tenure with about 84 years remaining.

The strata-titled structure will provide Tuan Sing with “significant and rare” flexibility in how it manages and positions the asset over the long term, the Singapore-listed firm said in an Oct 23 bourse filing.

This is given that the strata units can potentially be sold individually to realise and unlock value progressively, or the group could retain them as a whole for stable recurring income, depending on market conditions and its investment strategy.

The established office tenant base also enables the group to generate an additional source of rental income.

With the acquisition, Tuan Sing will strengthen its portfolio of income-generating investment properties in Singapore while increasing the group’s exposure to the Jurong Lake District, which is poised to become the country’s biggest business district outside of the CBD.

Its existing investment property portfolio in the city-state includes 18 Robinson with offices and retail spaces in the CBD, Dunearn Village shopping mall (formerly known as Link@896) on Dunearn Road, and The Oxley commercial and residential development in District 9.

William Liem, chief executive of Tuan Sing, described it as “a rare opportunity to acquire a high-quality Grade A commercial asset in Singapore at an attractive entry price”.

Westgate Tower’s agreed price tag of $600 million is below the independent valuation of the strata lots of $640 million as at Oct 1, 2026, determined using the income capitalisation method and discounted cash flow analysis. That works out to a discount of 6.25%.

The sellers of the two entities that own the strata units are a consortium comprising Low Keng Huat (Singapore) and Sun Venture Homes.

Back in 2014, the developers of the Westgate retail-and-office project — CapitaLand, CapitaMalls Asia and CapitaMall Trust — had sold the office tower to the consortium for $579.4 million. That translated to about $1,900 psf based on net saleable area.

Tuan Sing said its acquisition is expected to complete on Dec 1, 2026 or such other date as may be agreed between the parties.

title: Knight Frank's Nicholas Keong expands role to helm auction business; Christopher Loh joins Savills as facilities management head
article:
Real estate consultancy firms Knight Frank Singapore and Savills Singapore have separately announced personnel changes in their auction and facilities management businesses, respectively.

Nicholas Keong will now lead Knight Frank Singapore's auction business, in addition to his current role overseeing the business lines of prime residential sales and leasing, as well as private office.

The expanded responsibilities come as Tan Tee Khoon, head of auction and sales, has left to pursue other interests, the firm said in an Oct 23 release.

Tan was also head of the agency arm KF Property Network, which would close by the end of this year , Knight Frank had announced in July.

With Keong now as head of auction, residential and private office, the firm said it sees an opportunity to strengthen its residential platform “by bringing together three complementary business lines under a unified leadership structure”.

That will make Knight Frank better able to deliver integrated solutions to property owners, investors and high-net-worth clients, as well as unlock new growth opportunities, it added.

Low Kin Hon, interim CEO of Knight Frank Singapore, said: “Together, these teams support clients at different stages of their property journeys, from investment and acquisition through to leasing, disposal and portfolio strategy.”

In July, Low, who was then deputy CEO and head of valuation and advisory, took over day-to-day leadership of the Singapore business as interim chief after Galven Tan had resigned as Singapore CEO .

Meanwhile, another consultancy Savills Singapore on Oct 23 said it has brought Christopher Loh on board as head of facilities management (FM).

With the appointment, Savills aims to strengthen its integrated facilities management (IFM) capabilities and deliver innovative, value-driven solutions to clients.

Loh was previously with C&W Services Singapore, the facilities and engineering arm of Cushman & Wakefield, where he had spent nine years and was most recently managing director of facilities services.

With more than 25 years of experience in the built environment and facilities management sector, he has managed FM businesses generating more than $70 million in annual turnover and led over 600 professionals delivering IFM solutions in the government and institutional sectors.

His experience spans IFM, property management, asset management, project management, and leasing and tenancy management services.

In his new role, he will work closely with cleaning company Absolute Maintenance Services as well as mechanical and electrical engineering firm Alpina Holdings, which are part of the Savills group.

Cheng Su Chen, group managing director of IFM and facilities services at Savills Singapore, highlighted Loh’s extensive experience in leading large-scale facilities operations.

Marcus Loo, CEO of Savills Singapore, said: “Facilities management is an important part of Savills' broader real estate services offering, and we see considerable opportunities to strengthen this business as client needs become more complex.”

title: CapitaLand Investment appoints Hsieh Fu Hua as chairman, Png Chin Yee as director
article:
CapitaLand Investment Limited (CLI) has named finance veteran Hsieh Fu Hua independent chairman and non-executive independent director, effective Jan 1, 2027.

Hsieh is a director of GIC’s board and also co-founder and advisor to the PrimePartners Group and chairman of GXS Bank.

CLI has also appointed Png Chin Yee as non-executive, non-independent director. Png, president of Temasek Singapore, brings extensive leadership experience in investment management, finance, capital markets and corporate transformation.

The appointments follow the retirement of Miguel Ko as non-executive chairman and non-independent director, and Gabriel Lim as non-executive, non-independent director, upon the completion of their respective terms on Dec 31, 2026.

Ko will retire after 12 years with the group, having joined as CEO of Ascendas-Singbridge in 2014. Under his chairmanship, CLI evolved into a global real asset manager, expanding its institutional investor network and investment platform.

Meanwhile, Lim will have served the group for more than nine years, having joined the board of the former CapitaLand Limited in 2017.

"As CLI enters its next phase, our CEO, Lee Chee Koon, has my full support. I look forward to working closely with him and the management team to address our strategic priorities and execute them with discipline," said Hsieh in an Oct 22 release.

Ko expressed confidence in his successor, citing Hsieh's experience and judgement, as well as the continued support of CLI's board and leadership team.

title: Chinese market is gone for Western automakers, says Volvo CEO
article:
(Oct 23): Volvo Car AB plunged by about 30% to a record low after the Swedish automaker’s chief executive officer said the market for Western-developed cars in China is disappearing fast, prompting it to cut 2,500 more jobs.

Deliveries in China dropped more than 40% in the third quarter as local brands dominate the electric-vehicle market and a spending crisis weighs on demand. Volvo, owned by China’s Geely, is now valued at 29.8 billion kronor (US$2.68 billion or $3.83 billion), 80% less then when it listed five years ago.

“Nobody will be successful with the old recipe where you had global cars developed in Europe and sold them at a premium price” in China, chief executive officer Håkan Samuelsson said on Friday during an analyst call. “Those times are gone.”

The job cuts, affecting about 6% of Volvo Car’s workforce, are part of a plan to reduce costs by an additional five billion kronor. The latest round, targeting mostly Sweden, come on top of about 3,000 positions Volvo Car announced it would eliminate last year.

Volvo’s deeper savings measures mirror moves by manufacturers including Volkswagen AG and BMW AG, who are trying to become leaner to meet mounting Chinese competition. They are also stepping up local partnerships in China and development teams to come up with features to better target local tastes. Samuelsson’s comments suggest those steps may not go far enough.

BMW is set to start sales of its new iX3 sport utility vehicle in China next month, while the world’s biggest luxury-car maker in June slashed it outlook, citing dimming prospects in its biggest market. Volkswagen followed last month.

See also: Porsche locks-in on the super-sportscar segment with the Mission S

More than a hundred local brands are vying for buyers in China with the cut-throat competition forcing much fast model development times and lower prices. Western manufacturers like Volkswagen have been slow to react, and are lagging on some features favoured by domestic drivers, which have included gadgets like movie screens and advanced voice recognition.

Samuelsson admitted underestimating the rapid transformation of China’s car market. The Swedish brand, owned by China’s Zhejiang Geely Holding Co since 2010, will in future rely on technology and vehicle underpinnings from its Chinese parent to compete, Samuelsson said. Volvo, which listed in 2021, remains nearly 80% controlled by its parent, exacerbating share price swings.

“In China, you need to come back with regionally developed products with Chinese software, and there we of course have a huge advantage that we can work and develop those cars together with Geely,” he said during a Bloomberg Television interview.

See also: Performance Motors Limited introduces the PML One loyalty programme

Chinese brands are winning buyers with cheaper electric vehicles, advanced digital features and models tailored to local tastes. Western automakers, by contrast, have often relied on global models with higher prices and slower development cycles, leaving them struggling to keep pace.

Volvo’s troubles were evident when the company on Friday reported swinging to a loss that was much deeper than analysts had forecast. Aside from the issues in China, Volvo cited costs from tariffs in the US and the removal of electric-vehicle subsidies there.

To get back on track, the company plans to introduce seven new vehicles for Western markets and six regionally tailored models for China by the end of the decade.

In Europe, Volvo managed to grow sales even as competition there from Chinese brands is also intensifying. A European Union push to limit hybrid imports from the Asian country may provide only temporary respite as brands including BYD Co set up manufacturing in the region.

Samuelsson, who returned in April 2025 after leading Volvo for a decade through 2022, is preparing to hand over the CEO post to former Skoda boss Klaus Zellmer. The German manager is due to take over no later than Oct 1, 2027.

title: Turnover for 11 stocks with reduced board lot sizes traded 3.6% higher than broader STI stocks: SGX CEO
article:
The turnover for the 11 stocks selected for Singapore Exchange’s (SGX) 10-share board lot initiative is 3.6% higher than the broader stocks in the benchmark Straits Times Index (STI), says CEO Loh Boon Chye at the group’s 27th annual general meeting (AGM) on Oct 23.

The higher turnover reflects “broader participation”. SGX has also seen a greater proportion of individual participation, he adds.

On whether the bourse will consider further reducing the board lot size to one, Loh says it will be taken into consideration should there be a broader demand moving forward. He added that certain online and digital brokers’ platforms are already doing fragmented trading (double check if that’s the term).

SGX officially implemented the reduction of the standard board lot size for 11 counters on Oct 5. Securities priced $10 and above had their lot sizes reduced to 10 shares. The 11 counters are: DBS Group Holdings (DBS), Great Eastern Holdings, Haw Par Corporation, Jardine Cycle & Carriage (now Jardine Matheson Southeast Asia), Jardine Matheson Holdings, Keppel, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation (OCBC), Prudential PLC, SGX, United Overseas Bank (UOB) and Venture Corporation.

On Oct 6, SGX said the reduced board lots saw an “immediate uptake”. The 10-share lots were “the most common trade size” in nine of the 10 actively traded stocks, led by DBS with around 5,000 trades.

When asked about adjusting fee structures, Loh noted that several brokers have already made adjustments or introduced significant fee cuts.

See also: Are Singapore SMID stocks losing their allure?

Chairman Koh Boon Hwee said the group will work with the ecosystem, but added that SGX is “not in the position” to mandate fees for the broker system.

On tokenisation and the fractional trading of shares and options, Loh said the group is evaluating to implement the tokenisation of securities collateral. The group is also studying the real economic outcome brought about by fractical options and securities. On fractional shares, he pointed out that this is being offered by “quite a number of brokers” today.

Other questions at the AGM focused on the group’s capital expenditure for FY2027. SGX announced, in its FY2026 results announcement, that expenses for the next financial year will increase by 6% to 8% and capex will come in at around $100 million. At the time, SGX said the monies will be invested in strategic priorities, platform modernisation and capability.

See also: Shadows of Black Octobers linger, but rays of support seen from healthy earnings

When asked about the overall return on investment, Koh said investors should look at the group’s overall return on equity (ROE), which will give an idea of what the group has had to invest to achieve that. The money, he added, isn’t spent on creating new products, but underlying IT infrastructure including our efforts to ensure our platform is as safe as possible.

In terms of buybacks, Koh says the group tries to buy back sufficient shares for its stock programme so it doesn’t dilute its shareholders.

On future prospects, Koh notes that the geopolitical environment is going to be a “little more fragmented than we are used to”.

“It’s something we’re going to learn to navigate,” he says.

title: Seatrium to undertake conversion and integration works on five whale class powerships
article:
Mainboard-listed Seatrium has secured a contract to undertake major conversion work and integration of five whale class powerships for Turkish power generation company Karpowership. Seatrium’s scope of work encompasses equipment integration, mechanical completion and pre-commissioning works.

Powerships are floating power plants equipped with hydrogen-ready multi-fuel generation systems and integrated onboard substations that connect directly to national electricity grids. Seatrium will work on the third-generation vessels that deploy up to 600 MW of immediate, grid-ready power.

Alvin Gan, executive vice president for repairs and upgrades at Seatrium, says: “This significant milestone marks Seatrium’s first major conversion work and integration of Karpowership’s whale class powerships. We are proud to support Karpowership’s drive to pioneer innovative floating power solutions and the next phase of its fleet development, bringing our capabilities in complex vessel integration and offshore engineering to the project.”

Karpowership chief technical officer Gokhan Kocak says, “We are pleased to build on our strong partnership with Seatrium, whose proven expertise in complex vessel integration make them an ideal partner.”

The contract marks the next step following an earlier letter of intent (LOI) signed in August 2025, solidifying the long-term partnership between the two companies. The LOI had provided for three floating, storage and regasification unit (FSRU) conversions and the potential integration of up to six new-generation powerships.

title: UK said to push for carve-out from new EU tech sovereignty rules
article:
(Oct 23): The UK has voiced concerns that the European Union’s (EU) push for technological autonomy will damage British digital companies, arguing that it should be eligible to compete for contracts under forthcoming “Made in Europe” tech rules.

The EU is debating whether to limit contracts under its Cloud and AI Development Act to European companies, its latest push for European preference rules as it seeks to reduce its dependence on non-European providers, like the US, according to people familiar with the matter.

The proposal is the centrepiece of a sweeping “tech sovereignty” package being drafted by Brussels, which will create a tiered system for cloud computing services and software providers — dictating that European governments rely exclusively on EU vendors to handle their most sensitive data.

The two sides are intensifying discussions on this and other matters ahead of an EU-UK summit in Brussels on Nov 20.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has raised the prospect of Britain rejoining the EU in the future, sparking expectations of a reset in EU-UK relations 10 years after the Brexit vote. In a speech last month to Labour Party members, Burnham said that Brexit had left the country weaker and failed to allow Britain to “take back control” of its borders and rules, as promised by the Leave campaign.

However, the EU’s push for European preference across a range of legislative files, from cars to public procurement, has irked the UK.

See also: AI video startup Higgsfield draws investment from Nvidia

The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, did not immediately respond to comments. A UK government spokesperson said it’s closely engaging with the EU as the Cloud and AI Development Act develops, and will continue to make the case for close cooperation as a trusted partner. The spokesperson noted that the UK is already deeply integrated into Europe’s digital and technology ecosystem.

The new tensions over European preference rules center around two main objections from the UK side, according to people familiar with the discussions — the demand that digital services providers be physically based in the EU, and restrictions on ownership and control.

Britain is home to big telecommunications company and cloud providers, including BT and Nscale, which could be negatively impacted by the new rules.

See also: DeepSeek, MiniMax win approval for global use, state media says

Among the arguments made by the UK is that any move to exclude it breaches the terms of the post-Brexit trade deal that governs EU-UK relations, an argument refuted by the commission, according to people familiar with the matter.

The British government is under political pressure to align to Brussels on imposing tariffs on subsidised car imports from China in exchange for access to the EU-wide procurement model. France and Germany agreed a car deal last week which opens the door for the UK to qualify for European subsidies under “Made in Europe” rules set out by its forthcoming Industrial Accelerator Act. To benefit, however, the country will have to mirror EU’s rules on foreign direct investment and trade defence, a thinly veiled reference to measures the bloc has taken against China.

UK Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds signalled earlier this week he’s open to hitting Chinese electric vehicles with tariffs to win enhanced access to European markets, but would make the call based on UK needs not demands from the EU.

Among the other issues to be discussed at next month’s Brussels summit are greater alignment on rules governing transport of agriculture and food products, linking their cap-and-trade emissions programmes and greater access for young people to live and work in both jurisdictions, one of the most contentious aspects of the talks.

title: Eni raises investor payouts as high fuel prices boost cash flow
article:
(Oct 23): Eni SpA said it will return more cash to shareholders after the Middle East war drove up energy prices and sent refining margins soaring.

The Italian oil and gas producer will pay an extraordinary dividend of about €1.3 billion (US$1.5 billion) and increase its 2026 share buyback to €3.8 billion from €3.4 billion, according to a statement on Friday. It previously raised the buyback in April and again in July.

Europe’s oil companies have benefitted from exceptionally strong refining margins this year, with gains in prices for products such as diesel far outpacing those in crude. Milan-based Eni has also expanded its global oil and gas production portfolio and project ramp-ups are further buoying the bottom line.

Adjusted net income was €2.8 billion in the third quarter, beating the €2.5 billion average analyst estimate. Net cash from operations was €4.36 billion, compared with an estimate of €4.33 billion.

title: AI video startup Higgsfield draws investment from Nvidia
article:
(Oct 23): Higgsfield Inc, an AI video startup founded by a former Snap Inc executive, said it has attracted investment from Nvidia Corp and TCV to help fund global infrastructure and hiring to capture growing demand.

The San Francisco-based company has the majority of its engineering talent in Kazakhstan, and its announcement is part of Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s visit to the country. Billing itself as a specialist service for brands and creators looking to generate media and content at scale, Higgsfield said its registered users have grown to more than 40 million. The new funding is part of an extension to its Series B round in August, which raised US$400 million at a US$5.4 billion valuation led by DST Global. Higgsfield didn’t disclose the latest valuation or the size of the extension.

Video generation with artificial intelligence tools is notoriously capital-intensive, but startups in this sector have shown user engagement and drawn investor interest. China’s Kling AI, owned by Kuaishou Technology, this summer raised US$2.8 billion at about a US$15 billion valuation. Higgsfield’s US rival Runway AI Inc raised US$315 million at a US$5.3 billion valuation in February, which also had Nvidia participating.

Paying customers are increasingly joining AI video services like Higgsfield, which said it had added 10 million since its summer fundraising. TCV, a growth-stage fund that’s previously backed Netflix Inc, Spotify AB and ByteDance Ltd, said it’s investing in the AI video startup because it’s shown “a radically faster, professional-grade and AI-native mechanism for creators, brand marketers and agencies alike to turn ideas into images and video”.

Founded in 2023 by former Snap executive Alex Mashrabov and Kazakhstani AI engineer Yerzat Dulat, Higgsfield’s AI video-generation platform is on track to surpass US$1 billion in annualised revenue based on its current performance, Mashrabov said last month.

Higgsfield serves as a platform to access about 35 AI video models from other providers along with its own AI engine, allowing creators to access and combine those competing technologies. Users can select different models for various parts of a production, from storyboarding and character creation to audio and finished video.

See also: DeepSeek, MiniMax win approval for global use, state media says

title: SGX should begin planning ahead for ‘eventual transition’ in CEO role: SGX’s Loh Boon Chye
article:
Singapore Exchange (SGX) should begin planning ahead for the “eventual transition” for the role of CEO, announced CEO Loh Boon Chye at the group’s annual general meeting (AGM) on Oct 23.

“We are doing so from a position of strength – with a clear strategy, strong momentum and a highly capable leadership team. This gives us the opportunity to plan thoughtfully and with confidence for the future,” he says.

Loh, who was appointed SGX’s CEO on July 14, 2015, notes that his current contract runs until the middle of July 2027, which leaves the group with “ample time” to “plan thoughtfully” and work through the arrangements together. The group has not set a specific date for the transition.

What matters, Loh adds, is that the group gets the transition right, done in the “best interests of the company, our people and our shareholders - and keeping SGX’s momentum and ambitions firmly on track”.

“My ambitions for SGX are greater than ever. We have built the foundations to aim higher, move faster, and achieve much more. I want us to accelerate our growth, expand our global reach and take SGX to a new level. That is what I intend to drive forward,” he says.

“We have built something strong together. And I genuinely believe our best opportunities are still ahead of us,” he adds.

See also: XMH Holdings to appeal $10.2 mil tax bill for FY2024; slapped with $12.5 mil tax for FY2025

He lauded Loh’s achievements, noting that SGX was in the middle of a “crisis” when the CEO first joined.

“I remember reading about the outages. He worked really hard over the next two to three years to stabilise the situation, to ensure that our IT systems were up to snuff,” he said. “The fact that SGX had a relatively smooth ride on the IT front is a tribute to the amount of work he put in today.”

See also: Christie’s International Real Estate launches in the Maldives

Koh also highlighted Loh’s work in developing the strategy to transform SGX from a cash equities market to a global multi-asset platform.

“Derivatives, as we have discussed, is a really big part of the business,” he said.

“While things like ETFs and Singapore depositary receipts (SDRs) and other things are small today, don’t forget [that] all of these businesses start that way. Choosing not to do it is choosing not to participate,” he added. “While it has grown, we continue under Boon Chye’s leadership and look at emerging areas. He has articulated his confidence for some of these things in future.”

Koh also noted that Loh “isn’t going to go away anytime soon”. “Being the manager he is, he has definitely set into motion a transition that is going to be made as professionally as he can. And he has, especially in the last couple of years, set the foundations for the future in our cash equities market by his active participation first in the Equity Market Review Group and now in the EQDP.”

“We can continue to build on that, I believe that the company has done really, really well under Boon Chye’s leadership,” he added.

Since Loh’s arrival in July 2015, SGX’s shares, till June 30, are up 216%. Its NPAT is up 112% while the market cap for the group rose 252%.

title: DeepSeek, MiniMax win approval for global use, state media says
article:
(Oct 23): DeepSeek and MiniMax Group Inc have won approval to deploy models overseas, part of a wave of homegrown AI technologies that Beijing will allow to operate globally, a Chinese state media affiliate said.

Much of Chinese AI will remain free for export, according to a post published by Yuyuantantian, a social account affiliated with state broadcaster China Central Television. It addressed Beijing’s draft proposal last week for export control measures that would restrict certain artificial intelligence tools and services, including large language models and agents.

The proposed restrictions could limit overseas access to China’s most advanced models, potentially slowing an international surge in adoption driven by cost-effective Chinese open-source AI.

“Since the policy was announced, leading companies DeepSeek and MiniMax have successfully completed the registration process, as well as the procedures for open-sourcing and authorising overseas use,” according to the post published late Thursday by Yuyuantantian. “AI companies can continue their commercialisation efforts as usual.”

Chinese startups have made significant strides closing the gap on US market leaders this year. Beyond more affordable pricing, they’ve also attracted users by making their models easier to customise than proprietary systems like the ones on offer from OpenAI and Anthropic PBC. Beijing’s interest in controlling the export of what’s seen as strategically important technology has shown up most prominently in the way it forced the unwinding of Meta Platforms Inc’s acquisition of Manus, an AI agent startup with Chinese roots.

China regularly updates its catalog of technologies that are prohibited or restricted from export. In 2020, Beijing added algorithms to the list, after the first administration of US President Donald Trump threatened to ban TikTok unless the app sold its US assets to an American company.

See also: OpenAI shifts value to US$1.25 tril as funding talks finalise — Bloomberg

The latest revisions have been in development since the first half of the year, with government departments consulting and integrating feedback from research institutions and industry participants, Yuyuantantian said. The post stressed that the catalog aims to “define boundaries rather than simply restrict the export of AI technology.”

There are significant carveouts to the proposed regulations. Providing API access, web applications or software-as-a-service features will not be subject to export restrictions, even if powered by restricted underlying models, according to the post.

The post contrasted Beijing’s approach with that of Washington, accusing the US of using targeted export bans and technology blockades to protect its competitive dominance.

See also: Tesla’s lowered capex target fuels doubt on AI, robotics goals

“China, however, is not following this path,” the post added.

title: Apple is Wall Street’s favourite AI haven as spending fears hit
article:
(Oct 23): It’s become one of the most reliable trades in the stock market as sentiment towards artificial intelligence (AI) swings wildly: Whatever AI stocks do, Apple Inc does the opposite.

The iPhone maker’s stock is up 27% in 2026, making it the biggest contributor to the S&P 500 Index’s 12% climb. It’s also by far the best performer among the Magnificent Seven technology giants this year, a stark reversal from 2025, when its 8% gain put it near the bottom of the group.

The reason for the divergence is fairly simple. While most mega-cap tech companies are spending wildly on AI infrastructure, Apple is largely sitting it out and instead focusing on what it historically does best, creating products that get consumers buzzing, like its new foldable iPhone Duo. With Wall Street’s view towards AI capital expenditures seemingly in constant flux, the company’s shares have become investors’ preferred method for staying in Big Tech while avoiding some of the group’s ups and downs.

“Apple is a very liquid hedge against AI volatility, and it’s a great position to have if you are starting to get worried about AI but still want tech exposure,” said Jordan McCall, a senior portfolio manager at Russell Investments, which has US$434 billion ($555 billion) in assets and owns the company’s shares in multiple portfolios. “Apple is a flight to safety when the market gets nervous.”

The divergence was clear on Thursday, when Apple rose as much as 1% and was the only Magnificent Seven stock in the green, while the broader market fell with chip stocks leading the way down, after results from Lam Research Corp and Meta Platforms Inc raised questions about AI spending.

Investors are searching for safety because sentiment around AI is shifting so quickly. Shares of the big spenders like Microsoft Corp, Amazon.com Inc, Alphabet Inc and Meta Platforms Inc, and the chipmakers at the heart of AI infrastructure, rise and fall as Wall Street debates when and if the hundreds of billions in capital expenditures will pay off in a big way. Apple has an increasingly negative correlation to semiconductor stocks and often moves in the opposite direction of its mega-cap peers.

The dynamic was apparent last week, when concerns about cloud computing provider CoreWeave Inc’s debt spurred widespread selling of AI stocks. The SOX tumbled more than 11%, marking its worst week since April 2025, while an index of Magnificent Seven stocks sank 3.1%. Apple, meanwhile, rose 2% as the company said demand for the Duo was “nothing short of extraordinary”.

“If hyperscalers get more bad news, it would make sense to sell the SOX and use the money as a source of funds to buy Apple,” said Michael Matousek, the head trader of US Global Investors Inc. “Apple is more of a defensive play because it lacks exposure to the themes moving chips, and given how pronounced this kind of pair trade has become, it is so much easier to just go with the momentum. I wouldn’t fight it.”

See also: SK data centre arm in talks to fund US$350 bil AI buildout in South Korea

Apple’s 40-day correlation to the chip index has been negative since early July and is at its most extreme in data going back to 1994. On a 10-day basis, Apple has a negative 90% correlation with the chip index, according to Jonathan Krinsky, the chief market technician of BTIG.

Apple’s strong free cash flow and durable earnings growth are helping it stand out, McCall said. Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta have seen their free cash flow plummet or even turn negative as they invest in AI infrastructure. And while chipmakers are seeing huge growth for the time being, the fear is their earnings will nosedive if that spending slows.

The primary concerns for Apple shareholders are that it’s growing more slowly than its Big Tech peers but carries a soaring stock market valuation. The company is scheduled to report earnings for its fiscal fourth quarter in a few weeks, and revenue is expected to rise about 15% for the year, well below the overall tech sector, according to Bloomberg Intelligence data. What’s more, the pace is expected to slow to 9.7% in fiscal 2027 and to 5.5% in fiscal 2028.

Meanwhile, the shares trade at 36 times earnings estimated over the past 12 months, their highest multiple since January 2008. That’s twice Nvidia Corp’s valuation and well above where the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index and S&P 500 trade.

This combination could make it difficult for Apple to continue outperforming, especially if investors’ perceptions of big AI spenders and chipmakers improves again.

“With SOX having just seen a 16% pullback, and Apple at all-time highs, we think a bounce in SOX is likely to coincide with Apple pulling back, at a minimum, towards its 50 DMA,” BTIG’s Krinsky wrote on Oct 19, referring to Apple’s 50-day moving average, which was 4.7% below the stock’s most recent closing price.

There’s certainly a precedent for this kind of reversal. As recently as August, strengthening sentiment towards AI plays lifted shares of Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet, while Apple struggled.

“I would be shocked if we didn’t see another period of AI enthusiasm that leads to chipmakers coming back, and it is very reasonable and plausible to think the pattern would repeat itself again,” McCall said. “Risk on for AI would mean risk off for Apple.”
